newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Shevardnadze hails economy, electricity a worry.
newsitem.headline: Shevardnadze hails economy, electricity a worry.

text.p: Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze on Monday hailed his country's economic progress in the first half of 1997 as "wonderful" but said a deep energy crisis and budget woes needed to be fixed for continued growth.

Gross domestic product (GDP) soared 14.8 percent in the first half of the year compared to the same period in 1996, industrial production was up 11.8 per cent and inflation was held to just 3.4 per cent.
"These tendencies are wonderful, but we should pay special attention to the (1997) budget," said Shevardnadze in a weekly radio address.
Shevardnadze said that tax collection would have to be improved. Budget revenues were 85 percent of the target in the first half of the year.

Even more important, he said, was resolving the republic's severe energy crisis, which is a drag on enterprises especially during winter, when hydrostations which supply more than half of Georgia's energy are idle due to frost.
"If we don't have a strong energy base then the economy will not be able to grow and the reforms will end up being fruitless," he said.
Shevardnadze called for increased use of alternative energy sources such as wind and solar power.

Georgia's energy problems began when the Soviet Union broke up and it was forced to pay world prices for imports of natural gas and other fuels which it couldn't afford. Consumer and commercial debts led to debts of over $400 million to Turkmenistan for natural gas deliveries.
Georgia has the pipeline capacity to import as much gas as it needs but currently collects only 65 percent of tariffs owed from homes and businesses.
Georgia's economic growth in 1996 was the highest among former Soviet states at over 10 percent but this is partially explained by a very low base.
The Soviet collapse and myriad civil and ethnic wars in Georgia wiped out more than 80 percent of the economy from 1989 to 1994, when it hit rock bottom.
Most people in the Caucasus republic of six million still live below the poverty line.
